title: Steam Flow Measurement: 5 Proven Methods for Reliable Data

 Steam Flow Measurement: 5 Proven Methods for Reliable Data

 Steam is a compressible vapour whose density changes with every swing in boiler pressure, so a meter that ignores density can be wrong by ten percent or more. This guide shows how plants measure steam correctly, from vortex and orifice meters to full mass and energy compensation.

 
 Saturated and Superheated 
 Vortex and Orifice 
 Density Compensation 
 Mass and Energy 
 




 Steam carries most of the energy in a process plant, yet it is one of the hardest fluids to meter well. Good steam flow measurement combines the right primary element, careful installation and live density compensation.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how steam flow measurement works, which meters suit saturated and superheated steam, and how pressure and temperature compensation turn a raw signal into true mass flow.


 
 
 

 What Is Steam Flow Measurement?


 Steam flow measurement is the practice of finding how many kilograms of steam per hour pass through a pipe, using a primary element such as a vortex meter or orifice plate plus a density correction. Plants use the result for boiler efficiency, energy billing between units and boiler drum level control .


 Most flow sensors see velocity or volume, while the plant pays for mass and energy. That gap is the heart of the subject, and it is the same idea explained in mass flow versus volumetric flow .


 
 
 Image credit: Just Measure it . Image courtesy of Just Measure it, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 ICS Schneider Messtechnik notes that the same volumetric flow can represent a very different mass, and therefore a very different amount of energy, depending on the operating condition.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Saturated vs Superheated Steam


 Saturated steam sits exactly at its boiling temperature, so either pressure or temperature fixes its density. Superheated steam is heated above that point, so you need both.


 
 Saturated Steam

 
 Pressure and temperature are linked

 One pressure or temperature input is enough

 Common in process heating and tracing

 May carry water droplets (wet steam)

 
 

 Superheated Steam

 
 Temperature above saturation point

 Needs both pressure and temperature

 Common in turbines and long headers

 Dry, so fewer droplet errors

 
 




 ICS Schneider warns that a common setup error is to configure a meter for saturated steam when the line actually runs superheated, so the computed mass flow drifts quietly away from reality.


 Do You Know?
 At 10 bar gauge, saturated steam has a specific volume of about 0.177 cubic metres per kilogram, so its density is only about 5.65 kg per cubic metre. Water at room temperature is roughly 175 times denser.



 5 Proven Steam Flow Measurement Methods


 
 Vortex Meter
 A bluff body sheds vortices at a frequency proportional to velocity; multivariable models add a temperature sensor for density.
 Best for: saturated and superheated utility steam
 Popular 

 Orifice Plate with DP Transmitter
 A plate creates a pressure drop that varies with the square of flow, read by a DP transmitter.
 Best for: large lines, custody and boiler outlets
 Standard 

 Averaging Pitot or Annubar
 A probe senses impact and static pressure across the pipe diameter.
 Best for: big headers with low pressure loss
 Low loss 

 Spring Loaded Variable Area
 A cone moves against a spring and the DP across it is measured.
 Best for: wide turndown on plant steam
 Wide range 

 Insertion Turbine
 A small rotor on a probe spins with the steam velocity.
 Best for: large mains where cost matters
 Economical 




 The vortex principle is covered in detail in vortex flow meter working principle , and the differential pressure route in orifice plate flow measurement . An Annubar flow meter is a useful middle choice when pressure loss must stay low.


 Spirax Sarco notes that orifice plate turndown is limited to between 4:1 and 5:1 because flow follows the square root of differential pressure. The same guide quotes up to 100:1 turndown for spring loaded variable area meters and plus or minus 2 percent of reading for insertion turbines on steam.


 
 4:1 to 5:1 Orifice plate turndown 

 80 to 100 m/s Vortex upper velocity 

 100:1 Spring loaded variable area 

 5.65 kg/m³ Saturated steam at 10 bar g 




 Quick Tip
 Size steam meters on the minimum flow you must see, not only the maximum. Many boilers spend nights and weekends at 10 to 20 percent load, where an oversized orifice gives almost no usable signal.



 Vortex Meters for Steam Flow Measurement


 A vortex meter has no moving parts, tolerates high temperature and gives a frequency output that is linear with velocity. Spirax Sarco notes that vortex meters reach their maximum flow at velocities of 80 or 100 metres per second, while normal steam lines run much slower, which limits usable capacity at the low end.


 Multivariable vortex meters carry a temperature sensor in the shedder bar and compute saturated steam density for steam flow measurement inside the transmitter. For superheated steam a pressure input is also required, either built in or wired from a separate gauge pressure transmitter .


 Low velocity is the classic weakness, because shedding becomes unstable below a minimum Reynolds number at night time load.


 Orifice Plates, DP Transmitters and Condensate Pots


 For DP steam flow measurement, the impulse lines must stay full of water, never steam, so both legs read the same water head. Condensate pots at the tapping level provide that liquid seal, as described in condensate pot in steam applications .


 
 1
 Mount Taps Horizontally
 Use side tappings on horizontal lines so condensate fills both legs equally.


 2
 Fit Condensate Pots
 Install both pots at the same elevation as the tapping centre.
